t: Answer guest messages in your voice (save a skill)
lead: You'll build a saved skill that drafts replies to common guest questions in your company's voice, following your policies. Then you'll test it on two messages from the practice inbox.
why: Guests ask the same questions about check-in, pets and wifi every day, and reviewing a good draft takes seconds instead of minutes.
result: A saved guest-replies skill and two tested draft replies that follow your policies.

think.scene: At work: a reservations team answers most routine messages by reviewing a draft instead of typing from scratch.
think.ask: Which 5 guest questions do you answer most often?

steps.title: Describe your replies
steps.do: Paste this into your Cowork task. Replace the part in square brackets with your own 3 questions and policies, or keep the example, then press Enter.
steps.prompt: Help me build a skill called guest-replies that drafts answers to guest messages. Use the tone and never-rules in sample-business-brief.md in this folder. Our most common questions and policies: [e.g. 1. Early check-in: only if cleaning finishes early, never confirmed before 11am that day. 2. Pets: only at approved homes, with a fee. 3. Wifi: details are in the welcome book]. Keep replies friendly and short.
steps.see: Cowork asks you a question or two about your tone, or shows a draft of the skill listing your policies and the never-promise rules from the brief.
steps.stuck: If Cowork asks questions, answer them in the same task in a sentence or two. Leave out any real guest names, emails or phone numbers.

steps.title: Save the skill
steps.do: Paste this into the same task and press Enter.
steps.prompt: Save this as a skill called guest-replies so I can use it in future tasks. Then list the rules it will follow, in plain English.
steps.see: Cowork creates the guest-replies skill and lists its rules, including the never-promise rules. It may ask you to approve the skill or turn it on.
steps.stuck: If Cowork asks you to approve or turn on the skill, do that. If saving doesn't work, check Claude's help center at support.claude.com, or ask your Academy program contact.

steps.title: Test two messages
steps.do: Paste this into the same task and press Enter. guest-messages.txt, a practice inbox, is already in your Cowork Academy folder.
steps.prompt: Use the guest-replies skill to draft replies to messages 1 and 6 in guest-messages.txt in this folder. Show them here as drafts for me to review. Don't send anything.
steps.see: Two short drafts: one to Dana about early check-in that doesn't promise it, and one to Leo about his dog that follows your pet policy.
steps.stuck: If a draft promises something it shouldn't, paste: "That reply promised something it shouldn't. Add a rule to the guest-replies skill to prevent this, and save it."

steps.q: Your guest-replies skill drafts a reply to Dana, who asked for early check-in. The draft reads well. What do you do next?
options: Let Cowork send it, since the skill knows the policy
Read it, fix anything off, and send it yourself
Forward it to your manager to send on your behalf
steps.why: The skill drafts and you send, so a person stays responsible for every reply. Letting the skill send skips the check that catches the rare draft that gets a policy wrong.

t: Find what guests are really saying
lead: You'll have Cowork read a whole file of guest reviews, find the main themes and the properties with the most low ratings, then match those complaints to repair tickets.
why: Reviews show how to get more five-star stays, and linking them to maintenance shows which repairs are costing you ratings.
result: A one-page Word summary of review themes by property, matched to repair tickets, with 3 recommended fixes.

think.scene: At work: a team discovers that most low ratings at one property mention the same problem, and fixes it in a week.
think.ask: What do guests complain about that nobody has had time to count?

steps.title: Find the themes
steps.do: guest-reviews.csv is already in your Cowork Academy folder. Paste this into your Cowork task and press Enter.
steps.prompt: Open guest-reviews.csv in this folder. Find the top 5 themes in the comments, with how many reviews mention each. Then make a table of properties with review count, average rating and the number of reviews rated 3 or below, worst first.
steps.see: Five themes with a count for each, such as cleanliness, AC or door codes, and a table of the 12 properties with their average rating and low-rating count.
steps.stuck: If Cowork says it can't find the file, check that this task is using your Cowork Academy folder.

steps.title: Match reviews to repairs
steps.do: Paste this into the same task and press Enter.
steps.prompt: Now open maintenance-tickets.csv in this folder. For the complaints in reviews rated 3 or below, find repair tickets at the same property about the same problem. Which problems are hurting ratings and also costing us repairs? Show ticket counts and costs.
steps.see: A short list that links complaints to tickets at the same property, for example the AC at Driftwood Bungalow or the hot tub at Pine Ridge Cabin, with ticket counts and costs.
steps.stuck: If the matches look loose, paste: "Only count a match when the review and the ticket are at the same property and about the same problem."

steps.title: Write the summary
steps.do: Paste this into the same task and press Enter.
steps.prompt: Turn this into a one-page Word document called review-summary.docx in this folder. Include the 5 themes with a short guest quote for each, the properties that need attention, the review-to-repair matches, and 3 fixes that would raise our ratings. Say which fix would help the most.
steps.see: review-summary.docx appears in your Cowork Academy folder, with themes, quotes, the review-to-repair matches and 3 recommended fixes on one page.
steps.stuck: If the summary runs longer than a page, paste: "Cut this to one page. Keep the matches and the fixes."

steps.q: Your manager wants to visit the property with the most reviews rated 3 or below. According to your summary, which one is it?
options: Lakeside Retreat
Market Street Studio
Driftwood Bungalow
steps.why: Driftwood Bungalow has 6 reviews rated 3 or below, most about the AC. Lakeside Retreat has the lowest average (4.07) but only 4 low reviews, so the average alone points to the wrong house.

lead: You'll give Cowork the details for one property and get back a polished house guide as a Word document, plus a short pre-arrival message that points guests to it.
why: A clear house guide prevents the "how do I...?" messages that arrive after check-in.
result: A house guide Word document for one property and a matching pre-arrival message.

think.scene: At work: when every property has the same clear guide, the night-time "where is the...?" calls drop.
think.ask: Which property gets the most questions after guests arrive?

steps.title: Create the guide
steps.do: Paste this into your Cowork task. Replace the part in square brackets with real details for one property, or keep the example, then press Enter.
steps.prompt: Create a friendly, well-designed house guide for a vacation rental as a Word document called house-guide.docx, saved in this folder. Details: [e.g. Seabreeze Cottage in Harbor Point, check-in 4pm with door code sent the day before, wifi details on the fridge, 2 parking spaces, no parties, quiet after 10pm, beach is a 5-minute walk].
steps.see: house-guide.docx appears in your Cowork Academy folder, with clear sections such as Arriving, Wifi, Parking, House rules and Local tips.
steps.stuck: If you don't see the file, paste: "Where did you save house-guide.docx?"

steps.title: Review it as a guest
steps.do: Open house-guide.docx from your Cowork Academy folder and read it as if you were a guest arriving late at night.
steps.see: The guide opens in Word or your document viewer, with headings and your property details.
steps.stuck: If anything is wrong or missing, paste into the task: "Change [what to fix, e.g. check-in time to 3pm] and save the guide again."

steps.title: Write the welcome message
steps.do: Paste this into the same task and press Enter.
steps.prompt: Write a short, warm pre-arrival message I can send guests 2 days before check-in. Point them to the house guide and mention the 2 things they most need to know on arrival.
steps.see: A message of a few sentences in the task that you can copy into your messaging tool and send yourself.
steps.stuck: If it's too long, paste: "Make it 3 sentences."

steps.q: Your team is writing house guides for all 12 homes, and so far each one looks different. What's the best next step?
options: Save this format as a skill and reuse it
Copy this guide and edit the details by hand
Ask Cowork for a fresh design for every property
steps.why: A skill remembers the format, so every guide gets the same structure and you only supply the details. Editing copies by hand works for two or three homes, but layouts drift and details get missed.

t: Start the day with a sorted inbox
lead: You'll have Cowork sort a practice inbox of 8 guest messages by topic and urgency, then draft replies to the urgent ones for you to review.
why: Sorting an unsorted inbox at the start of every shift takes time you could spend helping guests.
result: A prioritized list of guest messages and 2 draft replies that only you send, saved for the next shift.

think.scene: At work: the morning shift starts with one prioritized list everyone can see.
think.ask: What would you do with the time you spend sorting messages each morning?

steps.title: Sort the messages
steps.do: guest-messages.txt, a practice inbox of 8 messages, is already in your Cowork Academy folder. Paste this into your Cowork task and press Enter.
steps.prompt: Open guest-messages.txt in this folder. Group the messages by topic and by urgency, and put anything that needs action in the next hour at the top. Don't send, change or delete anything.
steps.see: A grouped list, such as check-in questions, maintenance problems and booking requests, with the locked-out guests at Lighthouse View and the AC at Driftwood Bungalow flagged at the top.
steps.stuck: Want to try your real inbox instead? Only if your company has approved this connector. Otherwise, use guest-messages.txt. Only connect apps your company has approved, sign in yourself in the pop-up, and tell Cowork not to send, change or delete anything.

steps.title: Draft the urgent replies
steps.do: Paste this into the same task and press Enter. Read each draft carefully.
steps.prompt: Draft replies to the 2 most urgent messages. Show them here as drafts for me to review. Put a placeholder in square brackets for anything you can't know, such as a door code or arrival time. Do not send anything.
steps.see: Two drafts, one to Marcus at Lighthouse View and one to Grace at Driftwood Bungalow, with placeholders such as [new lockbox code]. Nothing has been sent.
steps.stuck: If a draft makes up a detail, such as a code or a technician's arrival time, paste: "Replace anything you guessed with a placeholder in square brackets."

steps.title: Save it for the shift
steps.do: Paste this into the same task and press Enter.
steps.prompt: Save the sorted list and the 2 drafts as morning-inbox.md in this folder, so the next person on shift can see what's handled and what's waiting.
steps.see: morning-inbox.md appears in your Cowork Academy folder, with the sorted list at the top and the 2 drafts below.
steps.stuck: If you don't see the file, paste: "Where did you save morning-inbox.md?"

steps.q: Cowork has drafted a reply to Marcus, who is locked out at Lighthouse View with his kids. The draft looks right. What happens next?
options: Tell Cowork to send it now, since he's waiting
You add the real code, then send it yourself
Approve it so Cowork sends similar replies next time
steps.why: Cowork drafts and you send, and here only you can supply the real code. Sending straight away feels faster, but a wrong or missing code would leave the family outside even longer.

t: Find the real cost drivers in maintenance
lead: You'll give Cowork the maintenance ticket log and find which properties, categories and vendors cost the most, which problems keep coming back, and what to fix first.
why: For operations coordinators and managers, maintenance logs hide patterns, like the same AC failing again or one vendor costing more per job.
result: Two charts and 3 preventive fixes based on patterns in the tickets.

think.scene: At work: an operations lead sees the same appliance failing month after month at one property, and replaces it instead of repairing it again.
think.ask: Which repairs feel like they happen over and over?

steps.title: Find the cost drivers
steps.do: maintenance-tickets.csv is already in your Cowork Academy folder. Paste this into your Cowork task and press Enter.
steps.prompt: Open maintenance-tickets.csv in this folder. Show which properties, categories and vendors cost the most, which problems repeat at the same property, and the average days open by priority.
steps.see: Tables of cost by property, category and vendor, a list of repeat problems at the same property, and average days open by priority.
steps.stuck: If Cowork says it can't find the file, check that this task is using your Cowork Academy folder.

steps.title: Chart it and recommend
steps.do: Paste this into the same task and press Enter.
steps.prompt: Make 2 charts that show the biggest cost patterns and save them in this folder as PNG images. Then recommend 3 preventive fixes, and tell me which 3 properties you'd visit first and why.
steps.see: Two chart images in your Cowork Academy folder, and in the task 3 preventive fixes plus 3 properties with a reason for each.
steps.stuck: If the charts appear only in the task, paste: "Save those charts as PNG files in this folder."

steps.title: Check a total
steps.do: Paste this into the same task and press Enter. Checking one number is a habit, not a sign of distrust.
steps.prompt: Double-check the total cost for the most expensive property against the raw file. List its tickets with their costs and add them up so I can check.
steps.see: That property's tickets listed with their costs and a total you could check in the spreadsheet yourself.
steps.stuck: If this total doesn't match the earlier table, paste: "These totals differ. Recount from the raw file and tell me which one is right."

steps.q: You can fund one permanent fix this quarter instead of another round of repairs. Which issue repeated most at a single property?
options: AC not cooling at Driftwood Bungalow
Hot tub not heating at Pine Ridge Cabin
Smart lock offline at Seabreeze Cottage
steps.why: Driftwood Bungalow logged 11 "AC not cooling" tickets, and it's the most expensive property at $14,563. The Pine Ridge hot tub gets talked about most, but it repeated 5 times.

lead: You'll build an interactive checklist that housekeepers tick off on every turnover, ending with a problem report for maintenance, and see how it works on a phone.
why: For operations coordinators and managers, a standard checklist means maintenance gets complete problem reports the first time.
result: A working turnover checklist page, with a problem report for all 12 properties, that opens on a phone.

think.scene: At work: housekeepers report problems the same way every time, so maintenance stops chasing missing details.
think.ask: What information does maintenance always have to chase housekeeping for?

steps.title: Build the checklist
steps.do: Paste this into your Cowork task and press Enter.
steps.prompt: Build an interactive turnover checklist for housekeeping at a vacation rental, as a single HTML file called turnover-checklist.html in this folder. Group tasks by room (kitchen, bathrooms, bedrooms, living area, outside), with tick boxes, a progress bar and large buttons that work on a phone.
steps.see: turnover-checklist.html appears in your Cowork Academy folder, and Cowork describes a checklist grouped by room with a progress bar.
steps.stuck: If you don't see the file, paste: "Where did you save turnover-checklist.html?"

steps.title: Add a problem report
steps.do: Paste this into the same task and press Enter.
steps.prompt: Add a "problems found" section at the end, with a property drop-down listing: Aspen Hideaway, Dockside Cottage, Driftwood Bungalow, Lakeside Retreat, Lighthouse View, Market Street Studio, Old Town Loft, Pelican Flats, Pine Ridge Cabin, Seabreeze Cottage, Summit Lodge, Willow Point House. Add a description box, a priority choice, and a button that makes a short maintenance summary I can copy.
steps.see: Cowork confirms the checklist now ends with a problems section that has all 12 properties, a description box, a priority choice and a summary button.
steps.stuck: If some property names are missing from the drop-down, paste: "The drop-down must list all 12 properties I gave you. Please fix it."

steps.title: Try it out
steps.do: Open turnover-checklist.html from your Cowork Academy folder. It opens in your web browser. Tick a few items, report a test problem and press the summary button.
steps.see: Items tick off and the progress bar fills. The button produces a short summary with the property, issue and priority.
steps.stuck: If ticking or the button does nothing, tell Cowork in the same task: "The checklist doesn't work when I open the file. Please fix it."

steps.title: Put it on a phone
steps.do: To see how a housekeeper would use it, save turnover-checklist.html to a shared drive your team already uses, then open it from your phone's web browser.
steps.see: The checklist fits your phone screen, with buttons big enough to tap.
steps.stuck: If your phone shows code or a download instead of the page, open the file in your phone's browser. If your team has no approved shared drive, ask your IT team how to share an HTML file, or skip this step.

steps.q: A housekeeper finds a leak under the sink at Lighthouse View. Why should she use the checklist's problem report instead of texting maintenance?
options: A text is slower to reach the right person in maintenance
Then maintenance no longer needs its own ticket log
Every report has the same details, every time
steps.why: A fixed format means each report has the property, issue and priority, so maintenance doesn't chase details. It doesn't replace the ticket log: the summary is meant to go into it.

lead: You'll have Cowork build an operations brief for one week from the bookings and maintenance files, check it, and then see how scheduling would repeat it every Monday.
why: For operations coordinators and managers, the Monday brief is built by hand every week. Checking it once, then scheduling it, turns that into a review job.
result: A checked weekly operations brief and a demo of scheduling it for Mondays.

think.scene: At work: the Monday meeting starts with everyone reading the same brief instead of someone building it that morning.
think.ask: Which numbers do you gather by hand before your weekly meeting?

steps.title: Build the brief once
steps.do: bookings.csv and maintenance-tickets.csv are already in your Cowork Academy folder. Paste this into your Cowork task and press Enter.
steps.prompt: Using bookings.csv and maintenance-tickets.csv in this folder, write a one-page operations brief for the week of 21 to 27 September 2026. Include arrivals that week by property, every ticket with status Open (oldest first, with days open as of 30 September 2026), and anything that could affect a guest's stay. Save it as ops-brief.docx in this folder.
steps.see: ops-brief.docx appears in your Cowork Academy folder, with arrivals by property, a list of open tickets starting with the oldest, and a short section on guest-affecting risks.
steps.stuck: If the list includes closed tickets, paste: "Only list tickets whose status is Open." For other changes, ask in the same task, for example: "Add the vendor for each open ticket."

steps.title: Schedule it
steps.do: This step shows the habit: check a report once, then let it repeat. When the brief looks right, paste this into the same task and press Enter.
steps.prompt: Create a scheduled task that rebuilds this operations brief every Monday at 7am from the newest bookings.csv and maintenance-tickets.csv in this folder, covering the most recent week in the data. Save it in this folder. Don't send anything.
steps.see: A confirmation of a weekly scheduled task for Mondays at 7am, with a short description of what it will do. Scheduled tasks may only run while your computer is on and the Claude app is open.
steps.stuck: If Cowork can't create a scheduled task, skip this step: the habit of checking once before repeating is the point. To learn more, check Claude's help center at support.claude.com, or ask your Academy program contact.

steps.q: Your brief lists the tickets still open on 30 September. Which open ticket has been waiting the longest?
options: Hot tub not heating at Pine Ridge Cabin
Lockbox code reset at Lakeside Retreat
AC not cooling at Driftwood Bungalow
steps.why: The Driftwood Bungalow AC ticket was opened on 31 August, weeks before the others. The Pine Ridge hot tub feels older because it keeps coming back, but its open ticket dates from 18 September.

t: Compare vendors with a research brief
lead: You'll compare your current HVAC vendors from the ticket data, then write a clear research brief so Cowork can find alternatives and put everything in one spreadsheet.
why: For operations coordinators and managers, vendors often go years without a check. A clear brief (goal, scope, sources, output) gets useful research in minutes.
result: A vendor comparison spreadsheet with your current vendors' costs, sourced alternatives and questions to ask before switching.

think.scene: At work: a purchasing decision that used to take an afternoon of browser tabs is ready before lunch.
think.ask: Which contract or vendor hasn't been compared in over a year?

steps.title: Compare current vendors
steps.do: maintenance-tickets.csv is already in your Cowork Academy folder. Paste this into your Cowork task and press Enter.
steps.prompt: Open maintenance-tickets.csv in this folder. For HVAC tickets only, compare each vendor: number of jobs, average cost per job, average days open, and which properties they served.
steps.see: A table of HVAC vendors, such as Coastal Climate Co. and Reliable Heating & Air, with jobs, average cost, days open and properties.
steps.stuck: If Cowork includes other categories, paste: "Only use rows where the category is HVAC."

steps.title: Send a research brief
steps.do: Paste this into the same task. Replace the part in square brackets with your area, then press Enter. You can do other work while it researches.
steps.prompt: Research brief. Goal: find 3 HVAC vendors that could back up or replace our current ones. Scope: [your area, e.g. the town where most of your homes are], home AC service with emergency call-outs. Sources: vendor websites and public reviews. Output: a table of published pricing, service area, review rating and contract terms, then questions to ask before switching.
steps.see: After a few minutes, a table of vendors with pricing, service area, ratings and contract terms, followed by a list of questions to ask.
steps.stuck: If it finds fewer than 3 vendors or the results are vague, change the area in the brief to the nearest larger town and send it again.

steps.title: Source it and save
steps.do: Paste this into the same task and press Enter.
steps.prompt: For each price and rating, add the source link or write "not found". Then save our current vendor comparison, the new vendor table and the questions as vendor-comparison.xlsx in this folder.
steps.see: vendor-comparison.xlsx appears in your Cowork Academy folder, with source links next to prices and ratings, and anything unconfirmed marked.
steps.stuck: If you don't see the file, paste: "Where did you save vendor-comparison.xlsx?"

steps.q: Before calling new vendors, your manager asks which current HVAC vendor costs more per job. What does the ticket data show?
options: Coastal Climate Co., at about $631 a job
Reliable Heating & Air, at about $631 a job
Reliable Heating & Air, at about $472 a job
steps.why: Coastal Climate Co. averages about $631 across 25 HVAC jobs, and Reliable Heating & Air about $472 across 29. Reliable did more jobs, which makes it easy to assume it costs more.

lead: You'll give Cowork the bookings export and find out where revenue really comes from: which channels, which months and which properties.
why: Knowing which channels bring the most revenue per night, not only the most bookings, changes pricing and marketing decisions.
result: Tables and charts of bookings by channel and month, plus 3 decisions the data supports.

think.scene: At work: a finance team sees that one channel brings more bookings but less revenue per night, and changes where it spends.
think.ask: What question about your numbers would you ask if analysis were free?

steps.title: Break it down

steps.prompt: Open bookings.csv in this folder. Show revenue, booked nights, revenue per booked night, average nightly rate, average lead time (days between booked_on and check_in) and cancellation rate, by channel and by month from April to September 2026.
steps.see: Two tables: one row per channel and one row per month, each with revenue, nights, revenue per night, average rate, lead time and cancellation rate.
steps.stuck: If Cowork says it can't find the file, check that this task is using your Cowork Academy folder.

steps.title: Make the charts
steps.do: Paste this into the same task and press Enter.
steps.prompt: Make charts of revenue by channel and revenue by month, and save them in this folder as PNG images.
steps.see: Chart images in your Cowork Academy folder, such as a bar chart by channel and a line or bar chart by month.
steps.stuck: If the charts appear only in the task, paste: "Save those charts as PNG files in this folder."

steps.title: Ask what it means
steps.do: Paste this into the same task and press Enter.
steps.prompt: Tell me the 3 pricing or marketing decisions these numbers point to. For each, say what would change your answer.
steps.see: Three decisions in plain English, each backed by numbers from the tables, with a note on what could make it wrong.
steps.stuck: If a decision isn't backed by a number, paste: "Show the figure from the tables behind each decision."

steps.q: Marketing wants to push the channel that earns the most per booked night. Which one does your table show?
options: Vrbo
Direct
Booking.com
steps.why: Direct earns about $298 per booked night, against $268 for Vrbo. Vrbo brings in the most total revenue, which makes it tempting, but per night Direct is worth more.

lead: You'll build an Excel model for one property that answers "what if?" questions about rates and occupancy, with working formulas you can change.
why: Testing a pricing decision in a model first is cheaper than testing it on real guests.
result: A working Excel model where changing an input updates every result.

think.scene: At work: a pricing decision gets made with a model everyone can see, instead of a gut feeling.
think.ask: Which decision do you make every season that a model could test first?

steps.title: Build the model
steps.do: Paste this into your Cowork task. Replace the part in square brackets with one property, or keep the example, then press Enter.
steps.prompt: Build an Excel model called rate-model.xlsx in this folder for [a property, e.g. Pine Ridge Cabin]. Inputs: nightly rate, occupancy, cleaning fee, platform fee percentage and monthly operating costs. Calculate monthly revenue and profit with working formulas. Highlight the input cells in a different color.
steps.see: rate-model.xlsx appears in your Cowork Academy folder. Cowork describes the highlighted inputs and the formulas for revenue and profit.
steps.stuck: If you don't see the file, paste: "Where did you save rate-model.xlsx?"

steps.title: Add scenarios
steps.do: Paste this into the same task and press Enter.
steps.prompt: Add a scenario table that compares: current numbers, rate up 5% with occupancy down 3%, and rate down 5% with occupancy up 6%. Show profit for each, using formulas linked to the inputs.
steps.see: Cowork confirms the file now has a scenario table with three rows and a profit figure for each.
steps.stuck: If the scenario numbers are typed in rather than calculated, paste: "Make the scenario table use formulas that update when I change the inputs."

steps.title: Change an input
steps.do: Open rate-model.xlsx from your Cowork Academy folder in Excel. Change the nightly rate and watch the results.
steps.see: Revenue, profit and every scenario update as soon as you change the rate.
steps.stuck: If nothing changes, the results may be typed in. Paste into the task: "Explain each formula in plain English, and fix any result cell that isn't a formula."

steps.q: Your manager changes the nightly rate in your model, and the profit cell doesn't move. What's most likely wrong?
options: The profit was typed in, not a formula
The file needs to be saved and reopened first
Excel needs a chart before results update
steps.why: A model works because results are formulas linked to the inputs. Saving and reopening won't help if the profit is a typed number, so check the cell's formula first.

result: An August 2026 performance report Word document and a saved monthly-report skill.

think.scene: At work: month-end reporting goes from a day of copy and paste to an hour of review.
think.ask: Which report would you most like to never build by hand again?

Include a short executive summary with total revenue compared with July, 3 charts inside the document, the top and bottom properties by revenue, and 3 recommendations.
steps.see: report-2026-08.docx appears in your Cowork Academy folder, with a summary, 3 charts, a property comparison and 3 recommendations.

steps.q: Before you share the August report, you check its headline number. What total revenue does August 2026 show?
steps.why: August 2026 brought in $82,754. $85,684 is July, the kind of month mix-up a quick check catches before others see the report.

lead: You'll have Cowork check a practice owner statement for Driftwood Bungalow against the bookings data, find the planted mistakes, and write a correction note.
why: Mistakes on owner statements are much cheaper to catch before they go out than after an owner calls.
result: A list of errors in the Driftwood Bungalow July statement and a correction note for you to review.

think.scene: At work: mistakes are caught before owners see them, not after they call.
think.ask: Which documents go out with numbers nobody double-checks?

steps.title: Check the statement
steps.do: owner-statement-driftwood-july-2026.csv is already in your Cowork Academy folder. It's a practice statement with mistakes planted on purpose. Paste this into your Cowork task and press Enter.
steps.prompt: Open owner-statement-driftwood-july-2026.csv in this folder. The management fee is 20% of rent. Check every row's math, compare each booking with bookings.csv, and look for duplicates. For each problem, give the booking ID, what's wrong, the correct figure and how you found it.
steps.see: A list of problems, each with a booking ID, what's wrong, the correct figure and how Cowork found it.
steps.stuck: If it finds fewer than 3, paste: "Check again, line by line: rent against nights times rate, the fee against 20% of rent, and every booking ID."

steps.title: Write the correction note
steps.do: Paste this into the same task and press Enter.
steps.prompt: Write a short note to the accounting team listing each correction on this statement, with the right figures and the corrected owner payout. Save it as statement-corrections.md in this folder.
steps.see: statement-corrections.md appears in your Cowork Academy folder, listing each correction with the right number, ready for you to review and send yourself.
steps.stuck: If the corrected payout looks off, paste: "Show how you calculated the corrected payout, row by row."

steps.q: Booking B1052 on the Driftwood statement has the wrong management fee. What should the fee be?
steps.why: The fee is 20% of rent, and B1052's rent is $466, so the fee is $93. The statement shows $117, which is 25%, and $95 is B1054's fee.

t: Rewrite a listing that sells (save a skill)
lead: You'll have Cowork critique and rewrite one property listing in your brand voice, then save the approach as a skill and test it on a second listing.
why: Strong listings lead with what guests care about, and a skill makes every new listing as good as your best one.
result: A rewritten listing and a saved listing-writer skill, tested on a second property.

think.scene: At work: every new property goes live with a listing that's as good as the best one in the portfolio.
think.ask: Which of your listings is underperforming and hasn't been touched in a year?

steps.title: Get a critique
steps.do: Paste this into your Cowork task. Replace the part in square brackets with one of your company's listing descriptions, then press Enter.
steps.prompt: Critique this vacation rental listing. What works, what's missing, and what would make a guest book? Listing: [paste a listing description here, e.g. Seabreeze Cottage, 2 bedrooms in Harbor Point. Near the beach. Sleeps 4. Wifi and parking.]
steps.see: A short critique with what works, what's missing, and specific suggestions such as moving the best features to the top.
steps.stuck: No listing handy? Keep the Seabreeze Cottage example, or copy a listing from your company's website.

steps.title: Rewrite it
steps.do: Paste this into the same task. Replace the part in square brackets with a few words about your brand voice, then press Enter.
steps.prompt: Rewrite the listing in our brand voice: [e.g. warm, relaxed, family-friendly]. Give me 3 title options and put the best features first. Never exaggerate distances or amenities.
steps.see: Three title options and a rewritten description that leads with the property's strongest features.
steps.stuck: If it adds a feature the property doesn't have, paste: "Only use features from the original listing."

steps.title: Save the skill
steps.do: Paste this into the same task and press Enter.
steps.prompt: Save your approach as a skill called listing-writer, including the brand voice and the rule to never exaggerate distances or amenities.
steps.see: Cowork creates the listing-writer skill and lists the rules it follows. It may ask you to approve the skill or turn it on.
steps.stuck: If saving doesn't work, check Claude's help center at support.claude.com, or ask your Academy program contact.

steps.title: Test on a second listing
steps.do: Paste this into the same task. Replace the part in square brackets with a different listing, then press Enter.
steps.prompt: Use the listing-writer skill to rewrite this listing: [paste a second listing here, e.g. Old Town Loft, 1 bedroom in Old Town. Walk to restaurants. Sleeps 2.]
steps.see: A rewritten second listing with 3 title options, in the same voice and structure as the first.
steps.stuck: If the style doesn't match the first one, paste: "Update the listing-writer skill so its output matches the first listing's style, and save it."

steps.q: Your rewritten Seabreeze Cottage listing says it's a 2-minute walk to the beach. The original said 10 minutes. What do you do?
options: Fix it to 10 minutes and update the skill
Keep it, since a shorter walk wins more bookings
Keep it, since booking sites verify distances
steps.why: A listing sets the guest's expectations, so a wrong distance wins a booking and loses the review. Booking sites don't check your walking times, so the fix and the skill rule are on you.

lead: You'll have Cowork research your local market, including demand drivers, events, competitors and typical rates, and turn it into a sourced one-page brief.
why: Walking into owner meetings knowing the local market makes your team more credible.
result: A sourced one-page market brief as a Word document.

think.scene: At work: the sales team walks into owner meetings knowing the local market better than the owner does.
think.ask: What would you want to know before your next owner or partner meeting?

steps.title: Research the market
steps.do: Paste this into your Cowork task. Replace the part in square brackets with a real town or area your company serves, then press Enter.
steps.prompt: Research the vacation rental market in [your area, e.g. the town where most of your homes are]: what drives demand, major events in the next 6 months, the main competitors and typical nightly rates by property size.
steps.see: After a few minutes, sections on demand drivers, upcoming events, competitors and a range of typical nightly rates.
steps.stuck: If the results are vague, use a smaller area, such as one town instead of a whole region.

steps.title: Ask for sources
steps.do: Paste this into the same task and press Enter.
steps.prompt: List the sources you used, with a link for each, and tell me which numbers might be out of date.
steps.see: A list of sources with links, and a note on which figures, such as nightly rates, may be old or estimated.
steps.stuck: If a number has no source, paste: "Find a source for that number, or mark it as an estimate."

steps.title: Make the brief
steps.do: Paste this into the same task and press Enter.
steps.prompt: Turn this into a one-page market brief as a Word document called market-brief.docx in this folder, with sources listed at the bottom.
steps.see: market-brief.docx appears in your Cowork Academy folder: a one-page brief with clear sections and a sources list.
steps.stuck: If it runs longer than a page, paste: "Cut this to one page. Keep the rates and events."

steps.q: You'll quote a typical nightly rate from your market brief in an owner meeting tomorrow. What do you do first?
options: Quote it, since Cowork found it online
Average it with our own rates from bookings.csv
Check its source and that it's current
steps.why: Web sources go out of date and can be wrong, so check any number you'll say out loud. Blending in practice data from bookings.csv would make the figure less reliable, not more.

lead: You'll have Cowork build a short PowerPoint deck that pitches your management services to a property owner, with a results slide built from bookings data.
why: A strong, consistent deck helps every salesperson pitch well, with numbers that back it up.
result: A 6 to 8 slide owner pitch deck as a PowerPoint file, with speaker notes and practice numbers clearly marked.

think.scene: At work: every salesperson pitches with the same strong deck, updated with fresh numbers each month.
think.ask: Which sales or owner meeting could a better deck change?

steps.title: Create the deck
steps.do: bookings.csv is already in your Cowork Academy folder. Paste this into your Cowork task. Replace the part in square brackets with your real fee, or keep the example, then press Enter.
steps.prompt: Create a 6 to 8 slide PowerPoint deck called owner-pitch.pptx in this folder, pitching our vacation rental management services to a property owner: the problem, what we do, how we price, results, next steps. Pricing: [your management fee, e.g. 20% of rent]; don't invent other fees. Results: revenue by channel and the top 3 properties by revenue from bookings.csv. Add speaker notes.
steps.see: owner-pitch.pptx appears in your Cowork Academy folder. Cowork lists the slides, including a pricing slide with your fee and a results slide with numbers from bookings.csv.
steps.stuck: If the pricing slide lists fees you didn't give, paste: "Only show the management fee I gave you on the pricing slide."

steps.title: Review the deck
steps.do: Open owner-pitch.pptx from your Cowork Academy folder and click through every slide, including the speaker notes.
steps.see: The deck opens in PowerPoint or Keynote with 6 to 8 slides and notes under each one.
steps.stuck: If a slide is too busy, tell Cowork in the same task: "Simplify slide [number, e.g. 3] to 3 short points."

steps.title: Mark the practice numbers
steps.do: Paste this into the same task and press Enter.
steps.prompt: Add a clear note on every slide that uses numbers from bookings.csv: "Practice data. Replace with our real, checked numbers before any owner sees this." Save the deck again.
steps.see: Cowork confirms the note is on the results slide and any other slide with practice numbers.
steps.stuck: If a slide with numbers has no note, paste: "Slide [number, e.g. 5] uses practice numbers too. Add the note there."

steps.q: Before you reuse the deck, you check the results slide against bookings.csv. Which property should top it by revenue?
options: Lighthouse View
Summit Lodge
Lakeside Retreat
steps.why: Summit Lodge earned $72,452, well ahead of Lighthouse View at $52,926. These are practice numbers, so swap them for your company's real, checked figures before a real owner sees the deck.

lead: You'll have Cowork pull one month of results and repairs for Driftwood Bungalow, then write an honest update letter to its owner that explains the repeated AC repairs and offers options.
why: Owners stay when they hear about problems from you first, with clear facts and choices, instead of finding them on a statement.
result: An owner update letter for Driftwood Bungalow as a Word document, with options for the AC.

think.scene: At work: an owner hears about a repeat repair from you first, with options and costs, instead of spotting it on a statement.
think.ask: Which owner would value a clearer monthly update from you?

steps.title: Gather the facts
steps.do: bookings.csv and maintenance-tickets.csv are already in your Cowork Academy folder. Paste this into your Cowork task. Pick July or August 2026 for the month, then press Enter.
steps.prompt: Using bookings.csv and maintenance-tickets.csv in this folder, summarize Driftwood Bungalow for [month, e.g. July 2026]: bookings, nights, revenue and cancellations, plus every maintenance ticket opened that month with its cost. Then list all its AC and thermostat tickets from April to September 2026, with the total cost.
steps.see: A short summary of the month, a list of that month's tickets with costs, and an AC history showing the same problems coming back.
steps.stuck: If Cowork mixes in other properties, paste: "Only use rows where the property is Driftwood Bungalow."

steps.title: Write the letter
steps.do: Paste this into the same task and press Enter.
steps.prompt: Write a short, warm, honest update letter to Driftwood Bungalow's owner as a Word document called owner-update-driftwood.docx in this folder. Cover the month's results, be open about the repeated AC repairs, and give 2 or 3 options with pros and cons. Don't invent prices: where a cost isn't in the data, write [quote needed].
steps.see: owner-update-driftwood.docx appears in your Cowork Academy folder, with the month's results, a plain account of the AC repairs and 2 or 3 options.
steps.stuck: If the letter softens the AC problem, paste: "Say plainly how many AC repairs there have been and what they cost."

steps.title: Read it as the owner
steps.do: Open owner-update-driftwood.docx from your Cowork Academy folder. Read it as the owner would, and check one number against the summary in your task.
steps.see: A one-page letter you could stand behind, with numbers that match the summary.
steps.stuck: If a number doesn't match, paste: "[the number, e.g. the July revenue] in the letter doesn't match your summary. Fix it." This is practice data: a real letter needs your real, checked numbers.

steps.q: The owner asks which problem keeps coming back at Driftwood Bungalow. What do the tickets show as the most repeated issue?
options: AC unit leaking
AC not cooling
Thermostat not responding
steps.why: "AC not cooling" appears 11 times at Driftwood Bungalow, more than any issue at any property. "AC unit leaking" is real too, at 6 tickets, so it's easy to mix them up.

lead: You'll have Cowork build a one-page KPI dashboard from the practice data, with key numbers, a monthly trend, a watch list that links low reviews to repairs, and a way to refresh it.
why: One page with the numbers you check most saves you from asking for reports, as long as you know how to refresh it.
result: A KPI dashboard HTML file with key numbers, a trend chart, a properties-to-watch list and a refresh habit.

think.scene: At work: leadership opens one dashboard, rebuilt from the newest data each week, instead of waiting for someone to build a report.
think.ask: Which 3 numbers would you want on one page every week?

steps.title: Build the dashboard
steps.do: bookings.csv is already in your Cowork Academy folder. Paste this into your Cowork task and press Enter.
steps.prompt: Using bookings.csv in this folder, build a KPI dashboard as a single HTML file called kpi-dashboard.html in this folder. Show 4 or 5 key numbers (revenue, booked nights, average nightly rate, cancellation rate) and a monthly revenue chart for April to September 2026. Add a short summary of what changed in September compared with August.
steps.see: kpi-dashboard.html appears in your Cowork Academy folder. Cowork describes number tiles, a monthly chart and a short September summary.
steps.stuck: If you don't see the file, paste: "Where did you save kpi-dashboard.html?"

steps.title: Add a watch list
steps.do: Paste this into the same task and press Enter.
steps.prompt: Add a "properties to watch" section. Use guest-reviews.csv and maintenance-tickets.csv in this folder to find properties where reviews rated 3 or below and repair tickets mention the same problem. Show the property, the problem, the number of low reviews and the repair cost.
steps.see: Cowork confirms a watch list with properties such as Driftwood Bungalow (AC) and Pine Ridge Cabin (hot tub), with low-review counts and repair costs.
steps.stuck: If the matches look loose, paste: "Only match a review and a ticket at the same property about the same problem."

steps.title: Open the dashboard
steps.do: Open kpi-dashboard.html from your Cowork Academy folder. It opens in your web browser.
steps.see: A page with the summary, 4 or 5 number tiles, a monthly chart and the watch list.
steps.stuck: If the chart is blank, tell Cowork in the same task: "The chart doesn't show when I open the file. Please fix it."

steps.title: Refresh by rebuilding
steps.do: This dashboard is a snapshot. It doesn't update by itself: you refresh it by asking Cowork to rebuild it from the newest files. Paste this into the same task and press Enter to practice.
steps.prompt: Rebuild kpi-dashboard.html from the newest bookings.csv, guest-reviews.csv and maintenance-tickets.csv in this folder. Show the last date in the data at the top.
steps.see: Cowork rebuilds the file. When you reload the page, the top shows that the data runs to 30 September 2026.
steps.stuck: Later, when you have a new export, save it in the folder with the same file name so it replaces the old one, then paste the same request.

steps.q: Leadership asks which month brought in the most revenue. What does your KPI dashboard show?
options: August 2026
June 2026
July 2026
steps.why: July 2026 was the top month at $85,684, a little ahead of August at $82,754. The two bars look close, so read the labels rather than judging by eye.

lead: You'll have Cowork interview you about a process your team runs every week, map it step by step, and mark where Claude could help and how many hours it would save.
why: The best automation ideas come from writing down how work really gets done.
result: A process map table showing which steps Claude could do and the hours saved per month.

think.scene: At work: mapping one weekly process often turns up hours of copy and paste that nobody planned.
think.ask: Which process does your team complain about most?

steps.title: Start the interview
steps.do: Paste this into your Cowork task. Replace the part in square brackets with a weekly process you know well, then press Enter.
steps.prompt: Interview me about a process my team runs every week: [e.g. preparing the weekly owner revenue updates]. Ask me one question at a time about each step, who does it, and how long it takes.
steps.see: Cowork asks you a first question, such as what starts the process or who does the first step.
steps.stuck: Pick a process you could explain in 5 minutes. If it's too big, choose one part of it.

steps.title: Answer the questions
steps.do: Type your answer to each question in the same task and press Enter. Keep going until Cowork says it has enough.
steps.see: A new question after each answer, and then a message saying it has what it needs to build the map.
steps.stuck: If you don't know how long a step takes, give your best guess and say it's a guess.

steps.title: Mark where Claude fits
steps.do: Paste this into the same task and press Enter.
steps.prompt: Map the process as a table: step, who does it, time it takes. Mark which steps Claude could do, which need a person, and estimate the hours saved per month.
steps.see: A table with one row per step, a column marking Claude or person for each, and an estimated monthly hours-saved total.
steps.stuck: If the estimate seems too high, paste: "Show how you calculated the hours saved."

steps.q: Your map of the weekly owner updates includes a step where someone decides whether to tell an owner about a big repair. Who should do it?
options: A person, since it needs judgment
Claude, since it can read every ticket faster
Claude, as long as it copies the manager in
steps.why: Good automation keeps people on decisions, approvals and relationships, and gives Claude the gathering and drafting. Copying a manager in doesn't make the judgment call any less important.

lead: You'll have Cowork prepare a 30-minute idea huddle for your team, then group and score the ideas and save the top 3 for the Spark your ideas mission.
why: Your team's best AI ideas come from the people closest to the work.
result: A huddle agenda and slide, a scored list of team ideas, and the top 3 saved in huddle-ideas.md.

think.scene: At work: when a manager asks for ideas every month, people start noticing the waste in their own work.
think.ask: Who on your team always has a better way to do things?

steps.title: Prepare the huddle
steps.do: Paste this into your Cowork task and press Enter.
steps.prompt: Create a 30-minute team huddle agenda and one simple PowerPoint slide called huddle-slide.pptx, saved in this folder, to help my team find ways Claude could save time in our work at a vacation rental company. Include 3 warm-up questions.
steps.see: An agenda in the task with timings and 3 warm-up questions, and huddle-slide.pptx in your Cowork Academy folder.
steps.stuck: If you don't see the slide file, paste: "Where did you save huddle-slide.pptx?"

steps.title: Score the ideas
steps.do: After your huddle, paste this into the same task with your team's ideas in the square brackets, then press Enter. Haven't run it yet? Keep the example ideas to practice.
steps.prompt: Here are my team's ideas: [e.g. draft replies to check-in questions; summarize open maintenance tickets each Monday; check owner statements against bookings; match low reviews to repair tickets]. Group them, score each by hours saved and effort, and pick the top 3.
steps.see: The ideas grouped by theme, a table scoring each one on hours saved and effort, and the top 3 picked out.
steps.stuck: If the scores seem off, tell Cowork what it got wrong, for example: "Owner statements take us 10 hours a month, not 2."

steps.title: Save the top 3
steps.do: Paste this into the same task and press Enter. You'll use this file in the Spark your ideas mission.
steps.prompt: Save the top 3 ideas to huddle-ideas.md in this folder. For each, write a clear title, the problem today, how Claude could help, and the estimated hours saved per month, in under 100 words.
steps.see: huddle-ideas.md appears in your Cowork Academy folder, with 3 short write-ups, each with a title, the problem, how Claude helps and an hours estimate.
steps.stuck: If you don't see the file, paste: "Where did you save huddle-ideas.md?"

steps.q: At your huddle, a housekeeper suggests an idea that would save her 20 minutes a week. What do you do with it?
options: Drop it, since bigger ideas matter more
Keep it on the list and thank her
Park it until bigger ideas come along
steps.why: Small ideas add up and show people their suggestions count. Parking it feels harmless, but people stop suggesting when their ideas disappear.

t: Write the leadership update in minutes
lead: You'll turn rough notes and numbers into a clear one-page leadership update, then save the format as a skill so next month takes one request.
why: Managers should spend their time on the decisions in an update, not on formatting it.
result: A one-page leadership update and a saved leadership-update skill.

think.scene: At work: managers spend their time on the decisions in the update, not on formatting it.
think.ask: Which update or report takes you longest each month?

steps.title: Write the update
steps.do: Paste this into your Cowork task. Replace the part in square brackets with your own rough notes, or keep the practice notes, then press Enter.
steps.prompt: Turn these notes into a one-page leadership update with wins, key numbers, risks and asks, in a clear and direct tone. Notes: [e.g. September revenue $53,501, down from $82,754 in August; Driftwood Bungalow AC: 11 not-cooling tickets since April; 12 tickets still open at 30 September; ask: approve replacing the Driftwood AC].
steps.see: A one-page update with four clear sections: wins, key numbers, risks and asks, using your notes.
steps.stuck: Rough notes are fine. If Cowork fills in something you didn't say, paste: "Only use what's in my notes."

steps.title: Test it
steps.do: Paste this into the same task and press Enter.
steps.prompt: What questions will my boss ask after reading this? Suggest how to answer each one in the update itself.
steps.see: A short list of likely questions, with suggested changes to the update that answer them.
steps.stuck: If the update grows too long, paste: "Cut it to half the length." Then decide what you miss.

steps.title: Save the format
steps.do: Paste this into the same task and press Enter.
steps.prompt: Save this format as a skill called leadership-update, so next month I can paste new notes and get the same one-page update.
steps.see: Cowork creates the leadership-update skill and describes its sections and tone. It may ask you to approve the skill or turn it on.
steps.stuck: If saving doesn't work, check Claude's help center at support.claude.com, or ask your Academy program contact.

steps.q: Your update is ready, and Cowork predicts your boss will ask why September revenue dropped. What do you do?
options: Add a one-line reason to the update now
Send it as is and answer in the meeting
Take out the September number to avoid it
steps.why: Answering the likely question in the update saves a round of back and forth and shows you've thought it through. Waiting for the meeting feels efficient, but it leaves readers guessing until then.
